learn.title: Input and output
learn.body: A function becomes powerful when it takes input and gives back a result. The input values are called arguments. The value handed back is the return value. Think of a function as a small machine.

learn.title: Take one, return one
learn.body: `int n` is a parameter. `return` sends a value back.

learn.title: Parameters and arguments
learn.body: In the definition, `int n` is a parameter, a variable local to the function. In the call, the 5 is the argument. When the function runs, `n` receives 5. The returned 25 replaces the call, so `a` is stored as 25.

learn.title: Two parameters
learn.body: The return type `double` matches the decimal result.

learn.title: Types must match the job
learn.body: The return type in front of the name says what kind of value comes back. Separate several parameters with commas and give each a type. Dividing by `2.0` avoids integer division, so 7 over 2 gives 3.5 and not 3.

learn.title: Arguments are copies
learn.body: C passes a copy of each argument. Inside `bump`, changing `n` changes only the copy. Back in `main`, `x` is still 5. To get a changed value out of a function, return it and store it: `x = bump(x);`.

questions.explanation: A parameter is the variable that receives the argument.
An argument is the value you pass in a call.

questions.prompt: `int x = 5; bump(x);` where `bump` only does `n = n + 1`. What is `x` afterwards?
questions.explanation: `bump` changed its own copy. The original is untouched.

questions.prompt: To send a value out of a function, use \_\_.
questions.explanation: `return value;` ends the function and hands the value back.

questions.prompt: What return type should a function have if it returns 3.5?
questions.explanation: An `int` return type would drop the decimals.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Arguments flow in as parameters, and the result flows out as the return value.
